newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi economy benefits from oil price windfall.
newsitem.headline: Saudi economy benefits from oil price windfall.

text.p: King Fahd and his advisers, economists and diplomats are sounding bullish again on the Saudi economy, but the world's largest oil producer remains vulnerable to the uncertainties of international oil prices.

So far, those uncertainties are all in favour of the desert kingdom, which depends on oil for 75 percent of its revenues and is the major beneficiary of an unexpected multi-billion dollar price windfall.
The $40 billion budget announced on January 1 assumed a price of $14 for every one of the eight million barrels of Saudi crude produced each day.

But the average price for this year has surged close to $18.50, giving Saudi planners a surplus of about $12 billion to factor into their calculations for dealing with a $4.9 billion 1996 budget deficit.
"The Saudi economy is strong and has firm bases," King Fahd said on the occasion of the Saudi national day last week.
Lower oil prices and the huge cost of the Gulf War produced cash flow problems for Saudi Arabia, launchpad for the U.S.-led coalition which drove Iraqi invaders out of Kuwait in 1991.
But economic reforms were beginning to bear fruit, Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Assaf told international bankers recently.
Gross domestic product growth was expected to be 6.2 percent this year compared with 4.2 percent in 1995.
"For '97, clearly things depend on developments in the oil market, but we are also optimistic," he said at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

Assaf later told U.S. business leaders that Saudi Arabia was determined to press ahead with reforms. A stable currency pegged to the dollar and low inflation estimated at 1.5 percent made for excellent investment opportunities.
Riyadh's ambassador in Washington, Prince Bandar, said the economy was improving and all indicators were heading in the right direction.
"I think we're seeing the end of the hard times," he told the U.S.-Saudi Business Council. The end of 14 years of deficit spending this year was in sight.
The deficits began in 1983 when oil prices began to fall, and ranged up to $20 billion before narrowing towards the end of the decade. They shot up again after the war.
Saudi Arabia's budget spending was under control, said Kevin Taecker, chief economist at Saudi American Bank.

"There's a strong commitment to fiscal discipline. This is now a $40 billion government, reduced from $60 billion over the last two years. That shows the strength of the economy. Show me any other economy that can cut its economy by 30 per cent without a depression," he told Reuters.

Taecker said the kingdom was building a clear vision for the future based on very realistic prospects for increasing the importance of the private sector while expanding the role of young Saudis in the kingdom's future growth and development.
"The outlook for the Saudi economy into the next century is full of potential promise," he said. "What really gives confidence is that big parts of visions for the future are filled in."
Despite a period of worry when King Fahd fell ill nearly a year ago with what was reported to be a stroke, important parts of economic momentum after the war were still in place.

Taecker said Saudi negotiations for membership of the World Trade Organisation, which requires disclosure of trade figures, and an invitation to join the Bank for International Settlements, which reflected its leading position among the economies of the Middle East, were signs of progress.

Taecker expects the government to use the oil windfall to reduce the budget deficit, settle its debts to contractors, help finance a $6 billion order for 61 airliners from Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp for loss-making Saudi Arabian Airlines, and fund new water schemes.
"The economy is definitely in better shape," said a treasurer with another Saudi bank. Government debts to the agricultural and medical sectors had been partly paid.
But Saudi Arabia had to build reserves. "You can't run a car very far with the petrol gauge warning light on," he said.
Diplomats who monitor the Saudi economy share the optimism.
"Agricultural bonds were redeemed in August, and outstanding payments to contractors are coming through. So there's a little bit of liquidity in the market," said one.
"The banks talk about being awash with funds. So things are looking good in the short term. They (the government) haven't got carried away with any big purchases like arms.
"Oil stocks are low and world demand is still increasing at 1.5 million barrels a day. In the longer term, Saudi Arabia is sitting pretty.
"In the medium term, however, the infrastructure built in the 1970s and 80s is going to need updating and replacing."

The private sector was being called in to help with funding for schools and health care, getting away from the concept that the Saudi state would provide everything from cradle to grave, another diplomat said.
The downside, despite oil reserves sufficient at present levels of production to last a century, was that the country remained vulnerable to price.
